newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: Albania anarchy hits ethnic Albanians' autonomy push.
newsitem.headline: Albania anarchy hits ethnic Albanians' autonomy push.

text.p: The near-collapse of Albania has deprived ethnic Albanian leaders in Macedonia and Yugoslavia of vital support for their drive for more autonomy, diplomats said on Monday.
"You could say the events in Albania have taken the wind out of their sails," said one diplomat.

"I do not believe leaders in Tirana, fighting for survival, will have time to spare for the problems of their ethnic kin across the borders for some time to come," Aleksandar Damovski, editor of the leading Macedonian opposition newspaper Dnevnik, told Reuters.

Until the Albanian crisis, the ethnic Albanian communities in Macedonia, and in Yugoslavia's troubled Kosovo province where Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, had been scenting progress in their struggle for autonomy.

The Albanian Party for Democratic Prosperity (PDPA) won the Macedonian towns of Gostivar and Tetovo in recent local elections. A drive by their mayors to join together the two ethnically almost pure communities angered Macedonian nationalists, to whom it smacked of secession.

Kosovo Albanians, having boycotted Serbian state institutions for the past six years, are facing important talks with their foes in New York in April, and sources said the status of the province will be on the agenda.

Diplomats say that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, having revoked the province's autonomy in 1989, could now bow to Western pressure and grant Albanians more autonomy in return for access to international monetary institutions, currently barred by a U.S. outer wall of sanctions.
"However, the collapse in Albania has opened a window of opportunity to Milosevic. He now has more time and more manoeuvring space," the Western diplomat said.

"We expect a more direct dialogue with the Albanians, now that Tirana is no longer in a position to champion the Albanian cause in the region," Macedonian Foreign Minister Ljubomir Frckovski told Reuters.

Publicly, ethnic Albanian leaders deny the events in Albania have had any impact on their struggle. "We have been isolated for fifty years and we have learnt how to fend for ourselves," said Arben Dzaferi, President of the PDPA in Macedonia.
But privately many voice concern: "This is profoundly disturbing. Our fight for human and other rights is difficult as it is without an uproar in Albania," said one ethnic Albanian leader.
Diplomats also note that Macedonian and some Kosovo Albanian leaders have made a tactical mistake by backing embattled Albanian president Sali Berisha against the rebels.
"Wrong move. They are cut off... Now they have to wait to see who wins and how the realignment of forces goes. All this takes time and energy," the diplomat said.

Dzaferi told Reuters his party's strategy was to "create a political crisis to prompt the Macedonian government into solving the existing problems." But with Tirana's political plate full, Macedonian officials believed he would have to back down.
"The debacle in Albania will contribute to a lessening of tensions and a softening of the rhetoric used by radical Albanians," a senior Macedonian official said.

To illustrate this, Frckoski warned the Albanians against radical steps: "For the time being our government is doing nothing. But the moment we see any action by the Albanians, we will move to sanction them radically," he said, though he did not elaborate.
